concepts.name: Ruff: `ruff check` vs `ruff format` in CI
A check fails CI through its exit code
Building the Docker image in CI
Branch protection with required status checks

questions.prompt: CI runs `ruff format --check .` and one file isn't formatted. What does Ruff do?

choices.text: Reformats the file and exits with code 0
Prints a warning and exits with code 0, so CI stays green
Leaves the file unchanged and exits with code 1, so the step fails
Exits with code 2, which means a configuration error

questions.explanation: With `--check`, Ruff writes nothing: it exits `0` when no file would change and `1` when some file would be reformatted. Exit code `2` is reserved for abnormal termination such as bad configuration. The non-zero exit is what turns the CI step red.

sources.title: The Ruff Formatter
sources.claim: With --check, ruff format writes no files and exits 0 when nothing would be reformatted, 1 when one or more files would be, and 2 on abnormal termination such as invalid configuration.

questions.prompt: After running `ruff format`, your imports are still in a messy order. Why, and what's the fix?

choices.text: The formatter doesn't sort imports; run `ruff check --select I --fix`, then format
Import sorting only runs with `ruff format --unsafe-fixes` enabled
Ruff can't sort imports at all, so you need to install isort alongside it
The formatter sorts imports only when `line-length` is set in `pyproject.toml`

questions.explanation: Import sorting is a lint rule set in Ruff (the `I` rules), not part of the formatter. The Ruff docs say to run the linter with `--select I --fix` and then the formatter. There is no need for a separate isort install.

sources.title: The Ruff Formatter
sources.claim: The Ruff formatter does not sort imports; the docs recommend running ruff check --select I --fix followed by ruff format.

questions.prompt: `ruff check --fix` fixes most violations but leaves one it says has a fix available. Why?

choices.text: `--fix` only fixes one violation per file per run
The rule isn't in the default rule set
Fixes are only applied when the formatter runs afterwards
That fix is unsafe (it may change behaviour) and needs `--unsafe-fixes`

questions.explanation: Ruff applies only safe fixes by default: ones that keep runtime behaviour the same. Unsafe fixes, such as rewriting `list(x)[0]` as `next(iter(x))` (which changes `IndexError` to `StopIteration` on an empty input), need `--unsafe-fixes`. Review those changes rather than applying them blindly.

sources.title: The Ruff Linter
sources.claim: Ruff applies only safe fixes by default; unsafe fixes such as RUF015's rewrite of list(...)[0] to next(iter(...)), which changes IndexError to StopIteration, need --unsafe-fixes.

questions.prompt: Why should CI run `ruff check` and `ruff format --check`, rather than `ruff check --fix` and `ruff format`?

model_answer.summary: CI should verify the committed code, not rewrite a throwaway copy of it: the checking forms exit non-zero on problems, while the fixing forms can pass while the repository stays wrong.
key_points: `ruff check` exits 1 when violations are found and `ruff format --check` exits 1 when a file would change, so the step fails
`ruff check --fix` exits 0 when it fixed every violation, so CI would pass
Fixes made in CI land only on the runner's copy, which is thrown away; the repository keeps the unformatted code
Developers fix locally (or with a pre-commit hook) and commit the result

questions.explanation: A CI check is a gate. It is only useful if it fails when the committed code is wrong. Fixing on the runner hides the problem: the job goes green and nobody commits the fix.

sources.title: The Ruff Linter
sources.claim: ruff check exits 0 when no violations are found or all were fixed automatically, 1 when violations remain, and 2 on abnormal termination.

sources.title: The Ruff Formatter

questions.prompt: You break a test on purpose and push. What exit code does `pytest` return, and what does GitHub Actions do with that step?

choices.text: Exit code 0, because the test run itself completed
Exit code 1; any non-zero exit marks the step failed and later steps are skipped
Exit code 1, but Actions only fails a step when it prints to stderr
Exit code 5; Actions retries the step once

questions.explanation: pytest exits `1` when tests were collected and run and some failed. GitHub Actions treats exit code `0` as success and any other exit code as failure, so the step, and with it the job and the pull request's check, goes red. Output on stderr alone doesn't fail a step.

sources.title: Exit codes
sources.claim: pytest exits 1 when tests ran and some failed, 4 on a command-line usage error, and 5 when no tests were collected.

sources.title: Setting exit codes for actions
sources.claim: Exit code 0 marks a step success; any non-zero exit code marks it failure, skips future steps and gives the check run a failure status.

questions.prompt: A typo in the CI command makes `pytest` look in a folder with no tests. What happens?

choices.text: pytest exits 0, because no test failed
pytest exits 1, the same as a failing test
pytest exits 5 (no tests collected), so the step fails
pytest exits 4 and prints its usage

questions.explanation: pytest has a dedicated exit code, `5`, for "no tests were collected". Because it's non-zero, CI fails, which is what you want: a green build that ran zero tests would be a false pass. Exit code `4` is for command-line usage errors.

sources.title: Exit codes
sources.claim: pytest exits 1 when tests ran and some failed, 4 on a command-line usage error, and 5 when no tests were collected.

questions.prompt: `def find_user(uid: str) -> User | None` is called as `find_user(uid).name`. Every test passes because the test data always has the user. Which CI step catches the bug?

choices.text: mypy, which reports that `None` has no attribute `name`
`ruff format --check`, because the call chain is badly formatted
pytest, which checks the return annotation at runtime on every call
The Docker build, which imports every module and would hit the error

questions.explanation: A type checker reasons about every path, including the `None` one no test exercises. mypy flags using `.name` on `User | None` until the code handles `None`. Python never checks annotations at runtime, so pytest only catches the bug if a test happens to hit that path.

sources.title: Kinds of types
sources.claim: mypy disallows most operations on unguarded optional (X | None) values and requires an explicit None check first.

sources.title: typing — Support for type hints
sources.claim: The Python runtime does not enforce function and variable type annotations; they are for type checkers and other tools.

questions.prompt: An interviewer asks: "What does your CI pipeline check, and why each step?" Answer for a pipeline with Ruff, mypy, pytest and a Docker build, and say why you order them that way.

model_answer.summary: Each step catches a different class of problem, and the fast, cheap checks run first so a pull request fails quickly.
key_points: Ruff lint and format checks catch style problems and common bugs such as unused imports, in seconds
mypy catches type errors, such as an unhandled `None`, on paths no test exercises
pytest catches behaviour regressions: the code runs but does the wrong thing
The Docker build catches packaging and Dockerfile problems that the tests, run outside the image, can't see
Cheap checks go first so a failure shows up fast, and every step fails the job through a non-zero exit code

questions.explanation: A good answer ties each step to the bug it prevents rather than listing tools. The steps overlap little: a formatter can't see a type error, and a type checker can't see wrong logic. Ordering by cost gives quick feedback.

questions.prompt: Your workflow uses `docker/build-push-action` with `cache-from: type=gha` and `cache-to: type=gha,mode=max`. What do these do?

choices.text: They push the image to GitHub Container Registry after each build
They reuse build layers from the GitHub Actions cache, and `mode=max` also caches intermediate layers
They cache only the final image's layers; `mode=max` sets the largest cache size
They cache the Python packages pip downloads, not Docker layers

questions.explanation: `type=gha` stores BuildKit's layer cache in the GitHub Actions cache, so unchanged layers aren't rebuilt. In the default `min` mode only layers exported into the final image are cached; `max` caches all layers, including those of intermediate build stages. Exporting needs write access to the Actions cache.

sources.title: Cache management with GitHub Actions
sources.claim: The type=gha cache backend stores and fetches BuildKit cache blobs via the GitHub Actions cache service, configured as cache-from: type=gha and cache-to: type=gha,mode=max, and cache-to fails where the workflow has only read access to the cache.

sources.title: Cache storage backends
sources.claim: In min mode only layers exported into the resulting image are cached, while max mode caches all layers including those of intermediate steps.

questions.prompt: You push the image only from `main`. Why still build it on every pull request?

choices.text: Branch protection can't require a check unless it builds an image
Building populates the registry so `main` can skip its build
The tests run inside the built image automatically
It catches a broken Dockerfile or a missing dependency before merge, not after

questions.explanation: Tests that run on the runner don't prove the image builds: a file left out of the build context or a missing system package only fails inside the Docker build. Building (without pushing) on each pull request makes that a red check you see before merging.

sources.title: Build context
sources.claim: COPY and ADD can only use files in the build context, and .dockerignore can exclude files from it, so a missing file fails inside the Docker build.

sources.title: docker/build-push-action: GitHub Action to build and push Docker images with Buildx
sources.claim: The action's push input defaults to false, so it can build an image in CI without pushing it to a registry.

questions.prompt: Branch protection on `main` requires the `test` status check. On one pull request the `test` job reports `skipped` because its `if:` condition was false. Can the pull request merge?

choices.text: Yes: a required check that is skipped counts as passing
No: a skipped required check counts as a failure and blocks the merge
No: GitHub first re-runs the job without its `if:` condition
Only an admin can merge it, by overriding branch protection

questions.explanation: GitHub lets a pull request merge when each required check has a successful, skipped or neutral status. So a required job that skips itself doesn't protect anything: keep conditions off the jobs you rely on as gates.

sources.title: About protected branches
sources.claim: Required status checks must have a successful, skipped or neutral status before changes can be merged into a protected branch.

questions.prompt: Explain how you would make sure a red CI run blocks merging into `main` on GitHub. Name the settings and one gap to watch for.

model_answer.summary: Protect `main` with a branch protection rule (or ruleset) that requires pull requests and the CI job's status check, keeps branches up to date, and doesn't let admins bypass it.
key_points: Add a branch protection rule or ruleset on `main` that requires a pull request before merging
Require status checks to pass and select the CI job's check by name
"Require branches to be up to date before merging" makes the checks run against the latest `main`
By default the rules don't apply to admins unless "Do not allow bypassing the above settings" is on
A required check that reports `skipped` still allows the merge

questions.explanation: CI only blocks bad code when branch protection makes its result a condition of merging. The strict "up to date" option closes the gap where two pull requests pass separately but break when combined.

sources.title: About protected branches
sources.claim: Protected branches can require pull requests and status checks, the strict setting requires the branch to be up to date with the base branch, and admins can bypass unless 'Do not allow bypassing the above settings' is enabled.

questions.prompt: Which Ruff check-mode facts support CI validation? Select all that apply.

choices.text: ruff check --fix always exits one even after fixing every violation.
A check-mode formatting failure means the repository is already formatted correctly.
ruff format --check reports needed formatting without writing files.
ruff check can return zero after --fix resolves every violation.
ruff format --check silently reformats files before returning success.

questions.explanation: a is incorrect: It can exit zero after all violations are fixed. b is incorrect: It means one or more files would change. c is correct: It exits one when reformatting would be needed. d is correct: A successful fix does not leave a failure exit. e is incorrect: Check mode does not modify them.

questions.prompt: Which CI exit-status statements are correct? Select all that apply.

choices.text: GitHub Actions treats every exit code as success if the script printed PASS.
A nonzero action exit code indicates failure.
pytest exits one when tests ran and some failed.
pytest exits zero when no tests are collected by default.
ruff check returns zero whenever lint violations remain.

questions.explanation: a is incorrect: Exit status, not that printed word, determines success. b is correct: GitHub marks the action check as failed. c is correct: That exit status reports failing tests. d is incorrect: Its default no-tests-collected status is five. e is incorrect: Remaining violations produce a nonzero exit.

questions.prompt: Which branch-protection choices can gate merging on CI? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Require named status checks to pass before merging.
Require branches to be up to date for strict status-check enforcement.
Requiring a pull request alone automatically requires every CI job to pass.
Protected-branch rules always prevent admin bypass under every default setting.
A red check blocks merging even when no applicable protection requires it.

questions.explanation: a is correct: Protected branches can enforce selected checks. b is correct: This checks against the current base branch. c is incorrect: Status-check requirements must also be configured. d is incorrect: Admins can bypass unless bypass is disabled. e is incorrect: Enforcement requires a relevant configured rule.

sources.title: About protected branches
sources.claim: Protected branches can require pull requests and status checks, the strict setting requires the branch to be up to date with the base branch, and admins can bypass unless 'Do not allow bypassing the above settings' is enabled.
